sentences.text: Acheroraptor was initially described as a mid-sized dromaeosaurid, a type of theropod dinosaur. The lead author suggested it was similar in size to Deinonychus, estimated at 3.3–3.4 meters long and weighing 60–73 kg, or up to 100 kg.

The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — consists of a nearly complete right maxilla with several teeth, showing minor damage and a missing section of the jugal ramus. A slight chin is present at the apex of the dentary, which is much weaker than that of Velociraptor.
The genus Acheroraptor contains only one species, A. temertyorum, which is based on an isolated maxilla with teeth.
Acheroraptor is one of the geologically youngest known dromaeosaurids, alongside taxa like Dineobellator and Dakotaraptor.

Acheroraptor was scientifically described in 2013 by Canadian paleontologists David Evans, Derek Larson, and Philip J. Currie. Fossils of Acheroraptor were first collected on 28 August 2009 by commercial collectors in the Hell Creek Formation, 45 km southwest of Jordan, Montana.

The discovered remains include a complete right maxilla (ROM 63777) and an assigned dentary (ROM 63778), both housed at the Royal Ontario Museum. The Royal Ontario Museum purchased the Acheroraptor fossils from a private collector.
Postcranial material, including three manual phalanges and a claw, was later assigned to Acheroraptor.
Analysis suggests Acheroraptor had relatively weak jaws adapted for rapid, slashing bites on smaller prey, similar to Velociraptorinae.
Acheroraptor belongs to the class Reptilia and the family Dromaeosauridae, a group of theropods found in the Americas, Antarctica, Asia, and Oceania during the Cretaceous.

Phylogenetic analysis recovered Acheroraptor as a member of the clade containing Eudromaeosauria and Microraptorinae, confirming its placement in Dromaeosauridae and possibly Eudromaeosauria. Two 2020 studies classified Acheroraptor as a basal member of the subfamily Velociraptorinae, extending the known range of this group to North America. Acheroraptor belongs to the parent group Velociraptorinae.
Acheroraptor lived in present-day Montana during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous period, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.

The fossils come from the upper part of the Hell Creek Formation, dating to the latest Maastrichtian stage immediately before the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event. The Hell Creek Formation environment where Acheroraptor lived was warm, humid, and swampy with maritime to subtropical conditions.
Average temperatures in the Hell Creek Formation ranged from 11.3 to 11.6 °C (52.3 to 52.9 °F). Cycads and Ginkgo trees were present in the Hell Creek Formation ecosystem.

The rivers and lagoons of the Hell Creek Formation hosted invertebrates, fish, amphibians, and reptiles including turtles, crocodilians, Champsosaurus, and mosasaurs. Diverse small terrestrial mammals and lizards lived alongside early snakes in the Hell Creek Formation. Pterosaurs found in the Hell Creek Formation include the azhdarchid Infernodrakon and an unnamed pteranodontian.

Palynological data indicates the Acheroraptor holotype locality comes from the lower-middle half of the Hell Creek Formation, not the upper half. While initially thought to come from the upper layer of the Hell Creek Formation, a 2020 abstract suggests Acheroraptor came from the lower layer.

Evans, Larson, and Currie (2013) concluded that Acheroraptor was the only dromaeosaurid from the Hell Creek Formation and that teeth previously attributed to Dromaeosaurus and Saurornitholestes actually belonged to it. The view that Acheroraptor was the only dromaeosaurid in the Hell Creek Formation was disproven in 2015 with the description of the larger Dakotaraptor.
